brand.name: aicourse.top
brand.sub: Learn to build with AI, from first principles
home.kicker: A free, open course in agentic engineering
home.h1: Every program is a list of steps.
home.h1b: The only question is who picks them.
home.lede: A complete course on building systems that use AI — written for people who are new to software engineering. Three parts, about four hours, and you finish having built a working agent with an eval suite that scores it.
home.free: No account. No ads. Anonymous page counts only. MIT licensed.
home.pathLede: Each part asks a little more of you than the last. Start at the top.
track.1.title: The Handbook
track.1.desc: Eleven illustrated sections on who decides the next step at run time — writing code, prompts, context, loops, graphs, harnesses, evaluation and security. Every model interaction here is a scripted simulation.
track.2.title: The Lab
track.2.desc: Four hands-on stages in this browser. Make a real model call, extend a rule-based till until it breaks, write your own prompt, then score it against twenty real cases and watch the number move.
track.2.meta: 40 minutes · your own DeepSeek API key · Provider charges vary
track.3.title: Build an Agent
track.3.desc: Nine guided stages (0–8), then a Stage 9 transfer project on your own machine. Build the model call, rules, prompt, evals, context, agent loop, controls and defences, then transfer them to a domain you know.
track.3.meta: 2–3 hours · TypeScript · offline or usage-based Provider calls
home.learnTitle: What you will be able to do
home.learn1: Tell which problems need a model and which do not
home.learn1d: The most valuable judgement in the field, and the cheapest to get wrong.
home.learn2: Write a prompt and prove it works
home.learn2d: Not by reading its answers — by scoring it against cases and watching a number.
home.learn3: Build an agent loop that survives failure
home.learn3d: Tools break. The loop has to read the error and adapt, not crash.
home.learn4: Put a fence around what a model can do
home.learn4d: Permission gates, mandatory review steps, and limits enforced in code.
home.for1d: Parts 1 and 2 assume no programming at all.
home.for2d: A full curriculum you can finish in an afternoon.
home.for3d: A 90-minute lesson plan, free to reuse and translate.
home.progNone: Nothing yet. Your progress is saved in this browser only — no account, nothing sent anywhere.
home.a1: Yes. The course is MIT licensed, with no account, email capture or advertising. The site keeps anonymous page-view counts without cookies or a personal profile. Part 1 is fully offline. Part 2 uses your DeepSeek key and can incur provider charges. Part 3 can run offline or use your own DeepSeek or Claude key.
home.q2: Do I need to know how to program?
home.a2: Not for Parts 1 and 2. Part 3 assumes you can read and write basic TypeScript — functions, objects, a for loop and await. If you cannot yet, do Parts 1 and 2 and come back. An older Python edition is preserved under legacy; TypeScript is the current course.
home.q3: Which AI model does it use?
home.a3: Part 1 uses scripted simulations and no provider. The browser Lab in Part 2 currently uses DeepSeek with your own key. The local TypeScript course in Part 3 supports DeepSeek, Claude or a scripted offline stand-in.
home.a4: The browser Lab keeps your key in session storage for the current tab and sends model requests directly to DeepSeek. The site does not intentionally send keys, prompts or replies to analytics. The analytics script runs on the same site, however, so it is a third-party trust boundary rather than a technical guarantee of isolation. Closing the tab forgets the local copy; it does not revoke the key at DeepSeek.
foot.licence: MIT licensed — use it, fork it, translate it, teach with it.
foot.disclaim: Not affiliated with any AI provider. All model behaviour shown is as of the model you run it on.
lab.keyNote: Held in session storage for this browser tab and erased when the tab closes. Current site code sends it only to DeepSeek. Vercel Analytics runs on this same origin and is therefore a third-party trust boundary; current site code does not send it your key, prompts or replies.
note.englishOnly: The teaching text in this section is currently English only. The interface is translated into nine languages; translating the long-form articles is the next job, and contributions are very welcome.
note.langHelp: Spotted a bad translation? Corrections are welcome — every string lives in one file.

ab.title: About
ab.lede: aicourse.top is a free, open course in agentic engineering, built by educational-technology researchers who work on how people actually learn.
ab.teamLede: Researchers whose work shapes how this course is designed and evaluated.
ab.why1: Most material on building with AI is written for people who already build software. That leaves out almost everyone who will have to work alongside these systems — teachers, students, analysts, anyone curious.
ab.why2: So this course starts from the only question that matters and never assumes you have written code before: every program is a list of steps, and the whole subject is who picks them. It is free, open source and translated into nine languages, because a paywall in English serves the people who need it least.
ab.how1: Every claim in the course is something you can run yourself. The eval suite is real, the agent loop is real, and the numbers you see are the numbers your own key produces.
ab.how2: The whole thing is MIT licensed and public. If something here is wrong, the fix is a pull request away.
ab.p.peter.aff: CEO and Founder, PedaNova Ed-Tech · Developer of 3D ENA 2.0
ab.p.peter.bio: Dr. Hu holds a PhD in Educational Technology from the University of Hong Kong and a BSc in Computer Science (machine learning and artificial intelligence) from the University of London. He builds theory-informed learning environments and analytical tools that connect educational research to working technology, and publishes in journals ranked among the top ten in Education and Educational Research by Web of Science. He wrote this course.
ab.p.hwang.bio: Prof. Hwang works on technology-enhanced learning: mobile and ubiquitous learning, game-based and flipped approaches, and artificial intelligence in education. His research links intelligent learning design to evidence-based teaching and assessment.
ab.p.tu.aff: National Taiwan University of Science and Technology
ab.p.tu.bio: Dr. Tu studies how generative AI and digital learning shape what learners perceive, do and achieve. She combines educational data mining, visual and network analysis, and mobile-learning research to make the process of learning visible enough to act on.
ab.p.yu.aff: 3D ENA Research Group, Hong Kong · BSc Computer Science, MA Psychology
ab.p.yu.bio: Mr. Yu brings together computer science and psychology to build interactive tools for epistemic network analysis and quantitative ethnography. He is the lead developer of 3D ENA 1.0, and applies network analysis to political discourse and social-media data.
lab.stepsLabel: The four steps of the Lab
lab.s1.name: Your first call
lab.s2.name: The wall
lab.s3.name: Write the prompt
lab.s4.name: Measure it
lab.nothingYet: The model's answer will appear here.
lab.setup.title: First, connect a model
lab.setup.lede: Three of the four steps below send your words to a real AI model and show you what comes back. For that the Lab needs a key of your own. It takes about two minutes, once.
lab.setup.whatIsBody: It is a long password that lets a program talk to an AI model on your behalf. You create one on the model provider's website, and it belongs to you, not to us. You pay the provider for real requests; the exact amount depends on model, time, cache use and returned usage.
lab.setup.s1d: Sign up and, if needed, add only an amount you are comfortable spending. The Lab shows request caps and an estimate before each paid action.
lab.setup.s2: Create a key and copy it
lab.setup.s2d: Copy the complete key. DeepSeek may show it only once; this Lab does not reject a key merely because of its prefix.
lab.setup.s3: Paste it in the box below
lab.setup.s3d: It stays in this browser tab and is erased the moment you close it.
lab.keyUnverified: Saved in this tab — not tested yet
lab.keyUnreachable: Saved, but the provider could not be reached
lab.keyModelVisible: GET /models accepted the credential and showed the selected model. It did not test account balance.
lab.keyRetained: The saved key was kept in this tab so you can test it again when the network is reachable.
lab.callPlan: Recommended journey: up to {calls} paid requests and {tokens} output tokens (1 + 3 + 28 + 28). Each extra evaluation can add up to 28 requests. Batches use concurrency 4.
lab.pricingDisclosure: Pre-run estimates use peak price, cache misses and the maximum output caps. Actual totals use returned usage. Price snapshot checked {date}.
lab.stopDisclosure: Stop prevents new requests and attempts to abort at most four already in flight. A request already sent may still be billed; without returned usage its cost stays unknown.
lab.forgetDisclosure: Forget removes this tab's saved copy only. It does not revoke the key in your DeepSeek account.
lab.err.noKey: This step needs your API key, and none is saved yet.
lab.err.unverified: Save & test the key for the selected model before starting a paid request.
lab.err.noKeyCta: Take me to the key box
lab.err.badKey: That key was not accepted. Check you copied all of it, with no spaces at either end.
lab.err.noCredit: The account behind this key has no credit left. Add a little on the provider's site, then try again.
lab.err.busy: The model is busy right now. Wait a few seconds and try again.
lab.err.network: The model could not be reached. Check your internet connection and try again.
lab.err.cancelled: This run was stopped. No score was created and your previous score was kept. Requests already sent may still be billed.
lab.err.content: The provider answered, but this case returned empty, truncated or invalid content. Its usage is still counted when the provider supplied it.
lab.err.generic: That did not work. The provider's own words are below, in case they help.
home.ideaLede: Every program is a list of steps. The only question is who chooses the next one, and when.
home.ideaAd: You write the steps in advance. The computer follows them exactly, every time — fast, predictable, and blind to anything you did not think of.
home.ideaBd: You describe the goal and let the model choose the next step while the program is running. Flexible, surprising, and it has to be checked.
home.ideaFoot: Almost every real system is a mixture of the two. Choosing the mixture is the whole job — and it is what you will practise here.
track.3.note: Starts with an on-site setup guide, then opens the local TypeScript course on GitHub.
lab.enData: The café orders, the menu and the twenty test cases stay in English. They are the exercise itself — the scoring compares the model's answers against English standards — so translating them would change what is being measured.
lab.draft.title: Local Lab draft
lab.draft.waiting: No local draft saved yet. Your first change will save on this device.
lab.draft.clear-failed: the saved draft could not be cleared
lab.draft.note: This device stores your current step, rules, full prompt and completed preview IDs in localStorage. The draft does not automatically copy the API-key field, model replies, raw errors, scores or billing. Anything you paste into rules or the prompt is stored as part of them, so do not paste secrets there. Current site code does not send the draft to Analytics; same-origin Analytics remains a disclosed trust boundary.
lab.draft.preview: {done} of {total} preview IDs saved locally; model replies are not saved.
lab.scaffold.title: Choose how much scaffolding you want
lab.scaffold.lede: Move from a complete example, to one missing condition, to a blank prompt whenever you are ready. These are choices, not locked levels.
lab.reflection.title: Before the Eval
lab.reflection.lede: Round {round} of 2: predict your score out of 20 and write one reason. The Eval button stays available if you skip this.
lab.reflection.reason: Why do you expect that score?
lab.reflection.private: Your prediction and reason are used only for this pause, then discarded when the Eval starts. They are never saved or sent to DeepSeek.
lab.reflection.twoDone: You have reached the two guided reflection rounds in this page session. Further Eval runs remain available.
lab.reflection.captured: Round {round} reflection fields completed; the text was discarded when the Eval started.
lab.reflection.optional: Round {round} started without both reflection fields complete — allowed, with no penalty.
lab.s1.lede: Before anything clever: prove the wire works. Ask the model anything, and watch what it costs — almost every tutorial hides that number.
lab.s1.callDisclosure: Run sends 1 paid request to {model} with a 250-token output cap. Peak/cache-miss estimate: up to about {cost}; actual cost uses returned usage.
lab.s2.lede: A till built the ordinary way — a list of rules a person wrote in advance. **Add rules until it handles all ten phrasings.** Real customers wrote them. Nothing on this step talks to a model, so it costs nothing.
lab.s2.ruleLimit: Rule limit reached ({limit}). Edit the prompt instead of adding more phrasing rules.
lab.s2.wall: **Look at what you had to write.** {rules} rules for ten sentences — and you had to think of each phrasing *before the customer did*. That is the wall. It is not a bug in your code; it is the shape of the problem.
lab.s3.lede: The same café till, but this time you describe the job in words instead of listing every phrasing. Write it, then try it on three real orders.
lab.s3.hint: You are the till at a small café…
lab.s3.callDisclosure: This preview sends at most 3 paid requests to {model}, each capped at 300 output tokens. Peak/cache-miss estimate: up to about {cost}; actual cost uses returned usage. You can stop the batch.
lab.s4.lede: Three orders is a feeling. Twenty is a number. Each case first generates an order; up to eight then need a separate judge. Run the whole set, then change one thing and watch the number move.
lab.s4.callDisclosure: One complete evaluation with {model} uses 20 generator requests (280-token caps) plus at most 8 judges (250-token caps): up to 28 paid requests, 7,600 output tokens, concurrency 4. Peak/cache-miss estimate: up to about {cost}; actual cost uses returned usage. A provider system error or Stop creates no score; invalid content fails only that case.
lab.s4.jump: **{prev} → {score}.** Same model, same twenty questions. The only thing that changed is that you told it what it was selling. **Most “the model is bad” is really “the model was never told”** — and you only know that because you had a number before and after.
lab.s4.resultMet: Evaluation complete: {score}/20. The suggested 16/20 target was met. Billing shown: {billing}.
lab.s4.resultBelow: Evaluation complete: {score}/20. The suggested 16/20 target was not met, but this complete Eval still counts as completed. Billing shown: {billing}.
lab.s1.q: Explain what an API is, to someone who has never written code. Two sentences.
build.title: Build the agent on your own machine
build.lede: Part 3 has nine guided TypeScript stages (0–8) plus a Stage 9 transfer project. This page gets the local tools working, proves offline Stage 0, and then hands you to the repository without pretending the website can see your progress.
build.repoLanguageBody: This launchpad is translated, but the Stage 0-9 repository lessons are currently in English. Commands and code stay unchanged.
build.stageMapBody: Open any stage in the repository. Work in order the first time; each link opens in a new tab.
build.stage2Title: Make the first real model call
build.stage9Title: Transfer the controls to your domain
build.copyFailure: Copy failed. Select the command and copy it manually.
build.boundaryTitle: A launchpad, not an online IDE
build.boundaryBody: Your code, model keys, outputs and progress stay in your local clone. This static website neither runs the course nor reads course/progress.json.
build.beforeTs: You can read and edit basic TypeScript: functions, objects, loops and await.
build.beforeTools: You have Git, Node.js 20.9 or newer, a terminal and a code editor.
build.beforeTime: Allow two to three hours for the nine guided stages (0–8); the Stage 9 transfer project is open-ended, and you can stop and return later.
build.cloneBody: Clone the public repository, enter it, and install the exact locked dependencies.
build.editBody: Open course/stage0-hello/run.ts and replace the empty QUESTION string with a question of your own.
build.offlineTitle: 3. Run and check it without a key
build.offlineBody: Offline mode uses a bundled deterministic stand-in. It is the safest preflight: no provider request, private recording or token charge.
build.successTitle: The check succeeds when you see
build.providerTitle: Choose a Provider only when you are ready
build.providerOfflineBody: Needs no key and makes no paid request. It proves the code path, but cannot demonstrate model variation.
build.providerDeepSeekBody: The default live Provider. Your terminal process reads DEEPSEEK_API_KEY; live stages incur DeepSeek charges and print their measured spend.
build.providerClaudeBody: An optional local Provider for comparison. Set the key and CAFE_PROVIDER. Claude pricing can be much higher, so inspect the printed estimate before a run.
build.costBody: Offline is free. Live totals vary with the selected model, tokens, cache and current Provider prices. Treat any course estimate as dated; the Provider dashboard is the billing record.
build.progressBody: The course checker writes course/progress.json locally. The website does not show a percentage, Resume or Completed state for Part 3 because it cannot observe that file.
build.artifactBody: Stage 9 asks you to move beyond the café and document an agent in a domain you know. A reviewable submission includes:
build.artifactBoundary: the problem boundary and what the model is allowed to decide;
build.artifactFailure: one realistic failure input that breaks the simple rules;
build.artifactEval: a small eval set with evidence, not just selected good outputs;
build.artifactGate: a code-enforced gate before the most irreversible action;
build.artifactTrust: the Provider, tool and untrusted-input boundaries;
build.artifactReview: a short retrospective on failures, trade-offs and the next test.
build.stuckTitle: If the local setup is too steep
build.stuckBody: Return to the browser Lab and practise rules → prompt → eval first. It teaches the same control handoff without asking you to install a development environment.
teach.title: Teach the control handoff
teach.lede: A printable teacher pack for 45, 90 or 180 minutes: a no-key route, classroom canary, disclosed call budget, learner worksheet and evidence-based project rubric.
teach.plan45: Feel the rules wall, watch a teacher-led prompt preview, run a baseline Eval, add context and compare the number.
teach.plan90: Add the Handbook vocabulary, loop and graph control, the security boundary and the decision tree.
teach.plan180: Let learners run the Lab with their own keys or the no-key route, play the Control Room, then begin local TypeScript.
teach.before1: Open the Handbook and Lab on the exact classroom browser and network.
teach.before2: For a live demo, create a separate low-credit key you can revoke; never share the teacher key.
teach.before3: Run Save & test, step 1, the three-order preview and one full Eval; compare usage and charge with the Provider dashboard.
teach.before4: Prepare the scripted/no-key route and switch to it if the live canary fails.
teach.noKeyTitle: The no-key route is a first-class lesson
teach.noKeyBody: Part 1 is scripted, offline and needs no key. In the Lab, step 2 is also local. Project the remaining model results or discuss a prepared run; do not troubleshoot private credentials in front of the class.
teach.callsTitle: Tell learners what a click can spend
teach.callsBody: These are maximum logical calls and output caps, not a price promise. Live cost depends on model, cache, time window and current Provider pricing.
teach.stopBody: Eval concurrency is 4. Stop prevents new scheduling and attempts to abort in-flight work, but an in-flight request may still be billed. A sent request without returned usage has unknown cost, not zero cost.
teach.work1: Write one phrasing the current rules miss and the extra rule it would require.
teach.work2: Before Eval 1, predict the score and give one reason.
teach.work3: Record the baseline, one failed case and the likely source of failure.
teach.work4: Name one change, predict its effect, then run Eval 2.
teach.work5: Record one improvement and one regression; do not hide inconvenient cases.
teach.work6: Transfer to a domain you know: one model decision, one retained control, one failure input and one irreversible gate.
teach.rubricBody: Score each criterion 0 absent, 1 partial or 2 evidenced. A different architecture can be excellent when the evidence and trade-off are defensible.
teach.rubricBoundary: Problem boundary: goal, non-goals and model authority.
teach.rubricFailure: Failure input: concrete, realistic and reproducible.
teach.rubricEval: Minimal eval: cases, expected evidence and an inspectable scoring rule.
teach.rubricGate: Irreversible gate: code or a person intervenes before the action.
teach.rubricTrust: Trust boundaries: Provider, tools, secrets and untrusted input.
teach.rubricReview: Reflection: failures, regressions, cost, trade-offs and the next test.
teach.evidenceTitle: Accept evidence, not one approved answer
teach.evidenceBody: Secret-free console output, a small JSON or Markdown result, a code link, one failed-case trace or a local report card can all be valid. The rubric does not require a particular framework, Provider or prompt.
teach.privacyBody: Keep pilot observation sheets local. Never put learner keys, prompts, raw Provider bodies, replies or identifiable work into this site, screenshots or CI logs.
